title: De Agri Cultura
text:
There are times when it would be better to seek a living by trade, were it not so hazardous, and likewise to lend money at interest, were it as honourable. Our forefathers held this view and laid it down in their laws, that a thief should be condemned to pay double, but a moneylender fourfold. From this one may judge how much worse a citizen they reckoned the moneylender than the thief. And when they praised a good man, they praised him in these words: a good farmer and a good husbandman; and to be praised in that way was held to be the highest praise of all. The merchant I consider to be energetic and bent on making his fortune, but, as I said above, his calling is perilous and exposed to disaster; whereas from the farmers come the bravest men and the most active soldiers, and theirs is the most respected, the most stable, and the least resented of all gains, and those who are engaged in that pursuit are the least disposed to evil thoughts. Now, to come back to my subject, what I have said will serve as a preface to my work.
1. When you are thinking of buying a farm, keep this in mind: do not buy hastily, do not spare your own pains in inspecting it, and do not think it enough to go round it once. However often you go, a good farm will please you the more each time. Take note how the neighbours keep up their places: in a good district they ought to be well kept up. Enter the farm and look about you, so that you will know how to get out again. See that it has a good climate and is not subject to storms; that the soil is good and strong in its own right. If you can, let it lie at the foot of a mountain, facing south, in a healthy situation, with a good supply of labourers and a good water supply, and a thriving town nearby, or else the sea, or a navigable river, or a good and busy road. Let it be among those farms that do not often change owners, where those who have sold their holdings are sorry they sold. See that it is well built. Do not rashly despise the experience of others. It is better to buy from an owner who is a good farmer and a good builder. When you come to the farmhouse, look whether there are many oil presses and storage jars; where there are not, you may be sure the yield matches them. There should not be much equipment, but the site should be good. See that the farm calls for as little equipment as possible and is not extravagant. Remember that a farm is like a man: however profitable it may be, if it is extravagant not much is left over. If you ask me what is the best kind of farm, I will say this: a hundred iugera of land of every kind, in the best situation. Of these the vineyard comes first, if it yields wine of good quality and in quantity; second, a watered garden; third, an osier bed; fourth, an olive grove; fifth, a meadow; sixth, a grain field; seventh, a wood for cutting timber; eighth, an orchard of trained vines; ninth, a forest of mast-bearing trees.
2. When the master of the household arrives at the farmhouse, after he has paid his respects to the household god, let him go round the farm the same day if he can; if not the same day, then the next. When he has learned how the land has been tilled, and what work has been done and what left undone, on the day after that let him summon his overseer and ask what work has been finished and what remains, whether the work has been completed in good time, whether what is left can still be finished, and what has been the yield of wine, grain, and everything else. When he has learned this, he should reckon up the labour and the days. If the work does not show, the overseer will say that he has done his best, but that the slaves have been sick, the weather bad, the slaves have run off, or that he has had to do public work. When he has given these and many other excuses, bring the overseer back to the account of work and labour. When the weather has been rainy, recall what work could have been done in the wet: the jars could have been washed and pitched, the farmhouse cleaned, grain shifted, dung carried out, a dung pit made, seed cleaned, ropes mended and new ones made; the slaves could have patched their own rough cloaks and hoods. On feast days the old ditches could have been cleared, the public road kept up, brambles cut back, the garden dug, the meadow cleaned, faggots tied, thorns rooted out, spelt ground, and general tidying done. When the slaves were ill, so large a ration ought not to have been given. When these matters have been gone over with a calm mind, see that whatever work remains is carried out. Reckon up the accounts of money and of grain and of what has been laid in as fodder; the accounts of wine and oil: what has been sold, what collected, what is left over, and what there is for sale. See that whatever security ought to be taken is taken, and that the rest of the stock is accounted for. If anything is wanting for the year, see that it is provided; let what is surplus be sold; let whatever is to be let out be let out; let him give orders for the work he wishes done and the work he wishes contracted, and leave these orders in writing. Let him look over the stock. Let him hold an auction: let him sell the oil if the price is right, the surplus wine and grain; let him sell the old oxen, the blemished cattle, the blemished sheep, wool, hides, the old cart, the old tools, the old slave, the sickly slave, and whatever else is surplus. The master of a household should be a seller, not a buyer.

title: De Agri Cultura
text:
3. In his early manhood the master of a household should devote himself to planting his land. As for building, he should think long before he builds; but as for planting, he should not merely think, but act. When he reaches the age of thirty-six, then he may build, provided he has his land planted. So build that the house does not have to look for the farm, nor the farm for the house. It is to the master's advantage to have a well-built farmhouse, an oil cellar and a wine cellar and many jars, so that he may be glad to wait for high prices: it will profit his estate, his honour, and his reputation. He should have good presses, so that the work can be well done. When the olives have been gathered, let the oil be made at once, lest it spoil. Remember that great storms come every year and are apt to bring down the olives. If you gather them quickly and your vessels are ready, no harm will come of the storm, and the oil will be greener and better. If the olives lie too long on the ground or on the floor, they will rot and the oil will be rancid. From any olives you may make greener and better oil if you do it in good time. To one hundred and twenty iugera of olive grove there should be two presses, if the grove is good and well stocked and well tended. There should be good crushing-mills, separate ones of unequal size, so that if the stones wear down you can change them; separate leather ropes; six levers; twelve fasteners; separate leather mainstays. Greek hoists are worked with two ropes of esparto: with eight pulleys above and six below you will raise faster; if you choose to fit them with wheels, the raising will be slower, but with less labour.
4. Have good stalls and good barred Faliscan mangers; the bars should be set a foot apart. If you do this, the oxen will not throw their fodder out. Build the town house according to your means. If you build well on a good farm, set it well, and live comfortably in the country, you will come oftener and more gladly: the farm will be better, less will go wrong, and you will get a greater yield. The forehead is before the back of the head: be a good neighbour, and do not let your household do wrong. If the neighbourhood is glad to see you, you will sell your produce more easily, let out your work more easily, and hire labourers more easily; and if you build, they will help you with their labour, their teams, and their materials; and if any need should arise, may it be a healthy one, they will defend you kindly.
5. These will be the duties of the overseer. Let him keep good discipline. Let the feast days be observed. Let him keep his hands off what belongs to others and guard his own carefully. Let him settle quarrels in the household; if anyone has done wrong, let him punish him in proportion to the offence and in good measure. Let the household not suffer want, cold, or hunger; let him keep it well employed, and so the more easily keep it from mischief and from meddling with others' property. If the overseer sets his face against wrongdoing, it will not be done. If he allows it, let the master not let it go unpunished. Let him show gratitude for good service, so that others may be glad to do right. Let the overseer not be a gadabout; let him always be sober; let him go nowhere out to dine. Let him keep the household busy, and see that the master's orders are carried out. Let him not think himself wiser than the master. Let him count the master's friends as his own. Let him obey the man he is told to obey. Let him perform no religious rite except at the crossroads festival, at the crossroads or at the hearth. Let him give credit to no one without the master's orders; what the master has lent, let him collect. Let him lend to no one seed grain, food, spelt, wine, or oil. Let him have two or three households from which he may borrow what he needs and to which he may lend, but no more. Let him reckon accounts with the master often. Let him not keep the same hired man, day-labourer, or caretaker longer than a day. Let him buy nothing without the master's knowledge, nor conceal anything from the master. Let him keep no hanger-on. Let him not consult any soothsayer, augur, fortune-teller, or astrologer. Let him not stint the seed corn, for that brings bad luck. Let him take care to know how to do all the farm work, and let him do it often, but not to the point of exhaustion; if he does this, he will know what is in the minds of the household, and they will do their work with greater contentment. If he does this, he will have less wish to gad about, his health will be the better, and he will sleep more soundly. Let him be the first to rise and the last to go to bed. Before that, let him see that the farmhouse is shut up, that everyone is asleep in his own place, and that the animals have their fodder.

title: De Agri Cultura
text:
See that the oxen are cared for with the greatest diligence, and humour the ploughmen somewhat, so that they may tend the oxen more willingly. See that you have good ploughs and ploughshares. Take care not to plough rotten ground, nor to drive a cart or stock over it; if you do not take care, wherever you drive, you will lose three years' yield. Bedding should be carefully laid for the cattle and oxen, and their hooves looked to. Guard against scab in the cattle and beasts of burden; it commonly comes from hunger and from rain falling on them. See that all the work is finished in good season, for farming is such that if you do one thing late, you will do everything late. If straw runs short, gather oak leaves and lay them down as bedding for the sheep and oxen. Take care to have a large dung pit. Keep the dung carefully; when you carry it out, clean it and break it up; haul it out in autumn. In autumn dig trenches round the olives and add dung. Cut leaves of poplar, elm, and oak in season; store them not too dry, as fodder for the sheep. Likewise the aftermath hay and the cuttings from the meadow; store them dry. After the autumn rain sow turnip, forage crops, and lupine.
6. As to where on your land you should plant, observe these rules. Where the soil is rich and fertile, without trees, that field should be a grain field. The same field, if it is misty, should be sown chiefly with turnip, radish, millet, and panic grass. In rich, warm soil plant the olive for preserving, the large radius, the Sallentine, the orcis, the posea, the Sergian, the Colminian, the white-wax olive, whichever of these they say is best in that district; plant that above all. Plant this kind of olive twenty-five or thirty feet apart. For planting an olive grove no land is good unless it faces the west wind and is exposed to the sun. Where the land is colder and leaner, the Licinian olive should be planted. If you plant it in rich or warm soil, the yield will be poor, the tree will exhaust itself in bearing, and a troublesome red moss will form. Round the borders and along the paths plant elms and some poplars, so that you may have leaves for the sheep and oxen, and timber ready if you should need it. Wherever in those parts there is a bank or a moist place, plant poplar cuttings and a reed bed. Plant the reed bed thus: turn the soil with the double mattock; there set the reed eyes three feet apart from one another. There plant wild asparagus, from which the asparagus comes, for it goes well with the reed bed, because it is dug and burned over and has shade in season. Plant Greek willow round the reed bed, so that you may have something with which to tie up the vine.
As to the land in which a vineyard should be planted, observe this. Where the place is said to be best for wine and is exposed to the sun, plant the lesser and the twin Aminnian, the lesser eugeneum, and the lesser helvolum. Where the soil is rich or rather misty, there plant the greater Aminnian, the Murgentine, the Apician, and the Lucanian. The other vines, especially the mixed kinds, suit any soil.
7. A farm near town is best suited to have an orchard of trained vines: wood and twigs can be sold, and there will be a supply for the master's use too. On the same farm each appropriate thing should be planted: the vine, the lesser and the greater Aminnian and the Apician; the grapes are stored in jars among the grape-skins; the same grapes keep well in boiled-down must, in fresh must, and in second wine. The kinds you hang up, the larger hard-skinned Aminnian grapes, or those kept at the blacksmith's, keep well in place of dried grapes. Plant or graft fruit trees: sparrow-apples, Scantian and Quirinian quinces, and other kinds for preserving, the early-ripening apples and pomegranates (for these you should apply hog's urine or dung at the root, to make food for the apples), the volaema pear, the Anician seedling pear (these will be good for preserving in boiled-down must), the Tarentine, the early gourd-pear, and as many other kinds as you can. Plant or graft olives, the orcis and posia kinds; these are best preserved either green in brine or crushed with mastic, or, in the case of the orcis, when they are black and dry, rubbed with salt for five days; then shake off the salt and put them in the sun for two days, or store them without salt in boiled-down must. Sorb apples may be preserved in boiled-down must or dried.

title: De Agri Cultura
text:
8. You should dry them. Do the same with pears. Plant the marisca fig in chalky, open ground; plant the African, the Herculanean, the Saguntine, the winter fig, and the black Tellanian with the long stalk in richer or manured ground. If you have a watered meadow, and it is not dry, sow it with grass so that hay may not run short. Near town have a garden of every kind, and every kind of plant for garlands, the Megarian bulb, the conjugula myrtle and the white and the black, the Delphic and the Cyprian and the wild laurel, smooth nuts, hazelnuts, Praenestine nuts, and Greek nuts; see that all these are planted. The farm near town, and that of the man who has only the one farm, he should so prepare and so plant as to make it as productive as possible.
9. Willow beds should be planted in wet, moist, shady places, near streams; and see to it that there is either use for them on the farm or that you can sell the produce. If you have water, make watered meadows by all means; if you have no water, make as much dry meadow as you can. This is the kind of farm it pays to keep wherever you have one.
10. How an olive farm of two hundred and forty iugera should be equipped. An overseer, an overseer's wife, five labourers, three ox-drivers, one ass-driver, one swineherd, one shepherd: thirteen persons in all; three yoke of oxen; three pack-asses harnessed to carry dung; one ass for the mill; one hundred sheep; five fully equipped sets of oil vessels; a copper kettle holding thirty quadrantals and its cover; three iron hooks; three water jugs; two funnels; a copper kettle holding five quadrantals and its cover; three hooks; one small basin; two oil amphorae; one fifty-measure urn; three ladles; one water bucket; one washbasin; one pot; one trulla; one little scuttle; one chamber pot; one watering-can; one ladle; one candlestick; one pint measure; three larger carts; six ploughs with shares; three yokes fitted with thongs; six sets of trappings for the oxen; one harrow; four dung hampers; three dung baskets; three pack-saddles; three pack-cloths for the asses; iron tools — eight forks; eight hoes; four spades; five shovels; two four-pronged rakes; eight hay-scythes; five straw-scythes; five pruning-hooks; three axes; three wedges; one mill for spelt; two pairs of shears; one fire-rake; two braziers; a hundred oil jars; twelve vats; ten jars for storing grape-skins; ten for lees; ten for wine; twenty for grain; one lupine vat; ten storage casks; one washing trough; one tub; two water troughs; separate covers for the jars and casks; one ass-mill and one hand-mill and one Spanish mill; three mill fittings; one table; two bronze platters; two tables; three large benches; one bench for the bedroom; three stools; four chairs; two armchairs; one bed for the bedroom; four beds with cords stretched across, and three other beds; one wooden mortar; one fulling-machine; one loom for weaving togas; two mortars; one mortar for beans, one for spelt; one for seed; one to sift kernels; one peck measure; one half-peck; eight mattresses; eight coverlets; sixteen pillows; ten cloths; three napkins; six patchwork cloaks for the boys.
11. How a vineyard of a hundred iugera should be equipped. An overseer, an overseer's wife, ten labourers, one ox-driver, one ass-driver, one willow-worker, one swineherd: sixteen persons in all; two oxen; two cart-asses; one mill-ass; three fully fitted press-sets; jars to hold five vintages, eight hundred cullei; twenty jars for grape-skins; twenty for grain; covers and lids for the jars, each its own; six esparto buckets; four esparto amphorae; two funnels; three wicker strainers; three strainers for skimming off the flower; ten must jugs; two carts; two ploughs; one cart-yoke; one wine-yoke; one ass-yoke; one bronze platter; one mill-fitting; a copper kettle holding one culleus and its cover; three iron hooks; a cooking-kettle holding one culleus; two water jugs; one watering-can; one washbasin; one pot; one ladle; one water bucket; one little scuttle; one ladle; one candlestick; one chamber pot; four beds; one bench; two tables; one platter; one clothes chest; one store cupboard; six long benches; one water wheel; one peck measure shod with iron; one half-peck; one washing trough; one tub; one lupine vat; ten storage casks; trappings for the oxen; trappings and three pack-cloths for the asses; three pack-saddles; three lees-baskets; three ass-mills; one hand-mill; iron tools — five rush-sickles; six woodland sickles; three pruning-hooks; five axes; four wedges; two ploughshares; ten forks; six spades; four shovels; two four-pronged rakes; four dung hampers; one dung basket; forty vine-knives; ten bush-knives; two braziers; two pairs of shears; one fire-rake; twenty Amerian baskets; forty seed-baskets or troughs; forty wooden shovels; two scoops; four mattresses; four coverlets; six pillows; six coverings; three cloths; six patchwork cloaks for the boys.

title: De Agri Cultura
text:
12. What is needed for the pressing-room. For five sets of vessels: five tempered press-beams and three spare; five windlasses and one spare; five leather ropes; five draw-ropes; five mainstays; ten pulleys; five head-stalls; five plank-rests on which the press-beams may lie; three storage casks; forty levers; forty wooden fasteners to bind the press-uprights if they spring apart, and six wedges; five crushing-mills; ten small tubs; ten troughs; ten wooden shovels; five iron shovels.
13. What is needed for use in the pressing-room. One jug; a copper kettle holding five quadrantals; three iron hooks; one bronze platter; mills; one sieve; one strainer; one axe; one bench; one wine-jar; one key for the press; one bed, made up, where two free watchmen may sleep (a third, a slave, to sleep together with the pressmen); new press-baskets, old ones; one running-rope; one cushion; lamps; one hide; two grills; one meat-rack; one ladder.
What is needed for the oil cellar. Oil jars; covers; fourteen oil vats; two larger and two smaller conchs; three bronze ladles; two oil amphorae; one water jug; one fifty-measure urn; one pint measure for oil; one small basin; two funnels; two sponges; two earthen jugs; two urn-measures; two wooden ladles; two keys with locks for the cellars; one balance; one uncertified hundred-pound weight, and the other weights.
14. If you let out the building of a new farmhouse from the ground up, the contractor should do the following. All the walls as directed, with lime and rubble; pillars of squared stone; all the necessary beams, sills, doorposts, lintels; supports and props; mangers for the oxen, winter and summer, Faliscan ones; a horse-stable; quarters for the household; three meat-racks; a round table; two copper kettles; ten pigsties; a hearth; a great doorway and a second one wherever the master wishes; windows; ten gratings for the larger windows, each two feet wide; six smaller windows; three benches; five chairs; two togas-looms; one small mortar where wheat may be pounded; one fulling-machine; door frames; two press-sets. For this work the master is to furnish the materials and supply what is needed, and provide one saw and one chalk-line (the contractor is only to fell, hew, and saw the timber and do the work), the stone, lime, sand, water, chaff, and earth from which mortar can be made. If the farmhouse is struck by lightning, this is to be a matter for negotiation. The price for this work, from a good master who supplies what is needed and pays the money in good faith, is two sesterces per roof-tile. The roof shall be reckoned thus: a whole tile shall count as one; one that is not whole, lacking a quarter, two for one; ridge-tiles shall count two for one; gutter-tiles, however many there are, shall count four for one.
For a farmhouse of stone and lime: the foundations are to rise one foot above ground; build the rest of the walls of brick, with such lintels and frames as are needed; for the rest let the rule be as for the lime-and-rubble house. The price is two sesterces per tile. The prices set above are for a healthy place and a good master; for the workmanship there will be an allowance to be agreed. For an unhealthy place, where the work cannot be done in summer, a good master should add a quarter to the price.
15. Walls of lime, rubble, and flint. The master is to supply everything for the work: five feet high, with a coping of one foot, one and a half feet thick, fourteen feet long, and the contract should specify that it be plastered. If he lets the contract for the farmhouse walls at a hundred feet — that is, ten feet each way, by the level, in courses of five feet — for one perch a foot and a half thick, ten sesterces. The master is to lay the foundations and supply for the work, for each running foot, one modius of lime and two modii of sand.

title: De Agri Cultura
text:
16. Those who give out the burning of lime on shares, give it out thus. The lime-burner finishes and burns it, takes the lime out of the kiln, and prepares the wood for the kiln. The master supplies the stone and the wood for the kiln, as much as is needed.
17. Oak timber, and likewise the vine-prop, is always ripe from the summer solstice to the winter solstice. Other timber that bears seed is ripe when the seed is mature. Timber that bears no seed is ripe when the bark peels. Because the cypress and the pine have green and ripe seed at once, you may gather their seed at any time of the year, and they too are ripe and seasonable at any time of the year. On the same trees there are two-year cones, from which the seed falls, and one-year cones; these last should be gathered as soon as they begin to gape. They first begin to ripen at seed-time, and afterwards remain ripe for more than eight months; this year's cones are green. The elm is ripe a second time when its leaves fall.
18. If you wish to build a pressing-room with four sets of vessels, so that they face each other, arrange the vessels in this manner. The press-posts two feet thick and nine feet high including the pivots; the slots three and a half feet long, cut out six inches deep, the first slot one and a half feet from the floor; between the posts and the walls two feet; between the two posts one foot; the posts set in a straight line up to the first standard, sixteen feet; the standards two feet thick, ten feet high including the pivots; the windlass, exclusive of the pivots, nine feet; the press-beam twenty-five feet long, including a tongue of two and a half feet; the floor for two sets of vessels, with two channels, thirty feet; the floor for the four crushing-mills, to right and left, twenty feet; the space for the levers between two standards, twenty-two feet; for the second set of vessels, on the opposite side, from the outermost standard to the wall behind the posts, twenty feet: total, for a pressing-room of four sets of vessels, sixty-six feet in breadth and fifty-two feet in length. Between the walls, where you are to set up the posts, lay good foundations five feet deep, and in them flint stones; let the whole bed be five feet long, two and a half feet wide, one and a half feet thick. There make a slot with two sockets, and set the posts on the socket in the stone. Between the two posts fill the remaining space with oak and pour in lead. Make the upper part of the posts six inches high, and set on it an oak capital, on which the standards may rest. Make foundations five feet deep, and in them set level a flint stone two and a half feet long, two and a half feet wide, one and a half feet thick; there set up the standards. Set up the other standard likewise. Over the posts and standards lay a level beam two feet wide, one foot thick, thirty-seven feet long; or use double beams if you have no solid ones. Beneath those beams, between the channels and the outer walls where the crushing-mills stand, lay a smaller beam twenty-three and a half feet long, a foot and a half thick, or put two in place of one. On these smaller beams lay the beams that stand above the posts and standards; on these timbers build up the walls and join them to the woodwork, so that it may have weight enough. When you make the basin, lay foundations five feet deep and six feet wide, and make the round basin and channel four and a half feet wide; for all the rest of the floor lay foundations two feet deep. First ram the foundations, then build them up in layers of half a foot each, with small rubble and lime mortar. Make the floors thus: when you have levelled, lay a first layer of gravel and lime mortar, beat it down with rammers, and make a second layer of the same; on this lay sifted lime two inches deep, and on that build the floor of dry potsherd; when it is built, ram and rub it smooth, so that it may be a good floor. Make the posts and standards of oak or pine. If you wish to make the beams shorter, finish off the channels outside the column; if you do so, the beams need be only twenty-two feet long. Make a press-board four feet wide, of Punic jointing, six inches thick; fit oak dovetails into it; when you have fastened them, secure them with pegs of cornel-wood. Into that board set three chains, and fasten the chains to the board with iron nails. Make the board of elm or hazel; if you have both, use them alternately.

title: De Agri Cultura
text:
19. For the wine vessels make the standards and posts two feet higher; above the slots of the posts, leaving a foot's space each way, make room for one fastener. Bore six holes half a foot apart each way in the windlass. Make the first hole half a foot from the pivot, and space the rest as evenly as possible. Make a peg-stop in the middle of the windlass. Whatever the midpoint is between the posts, level it to the centre where the peg-stop is to be fixed, so that the press-beam may rest truly in the middle. When you make the tongue, level it from the middle of the press-beam, so that it fits well between the posts; allow a thumb's breadth of play. The longest levers eighteen feet, the second sixteen feet, the third fifteen feet; the release-levers twelve feet, others ten, others eight.
20. How a crushing-mill should be put together. The iron pivot that stands in the central pillar should stand upright in the middle, true to the plumb-line; it should be well fixed round about with willow wedges, and lead poured in; take care that the pivot does not wobble. If it shifts, take it out, and do it again the same way, so that it does not move. Make the bearings in the wheels of oleaster wood from the orcis olive; cover them round with lead; take care they are not loose. Set them in the bar. Make the keys solid, a thumb-breadth wide; let them have a double lip, which you may fix with double nails so that they do not fall out.
21. Make the bar ten feet long, as thick as the bearings require, and let the middle part, which lies between the wheels, fit them. Pierce the middle, as wide as the iron pivot will be, so that you can insert the pivot. Into it set an iron pipe that fits both the pivot and the bar. Bore through the bar, right and left, four first-finger-breadths wide and three first-finger-breadths deep, and under the bar fasten an iron plate, as wide as the middle of the bar, pierced to fit the pivot. Where you have made the holes, right and left, bind them round with plates. Fold all four plates over onto the under part of the bar; on each side, beneath the plates, put little plates fixed to one another, so that the holes do not grow larger, into which the smaller bushings are set. Where the bar ends in the bearings, on each side make four iron tiles of your own to fasten there. Fasten the middle of the tiles with little nails. Above the tiles, on the outside, bore through the bar where the bolt is to pass that closes the wheel. Above the hole set an iron weight-plate six inches wide, pierced on both sides where the bolt passes. All this is done so that the bar may not be worn down on the stone. Make four rings to set round the wheel, so that the bar and the bolt may not be worn on the inside. Make the bar of elm or beech wood. Let the same smith make and fasten the ironwork that is needed: sixty pounds are needed. Buy four pounds of lead for the bar. For the workman who puts the bar together, sets in the bearings and runs in the lead, count eight days of a smith's labour: the same man should fit the crushing-mill. Total cost, seventy-two sesterces, besides the assistants.
22. The crushing-mill should be fitted thus. The fitter should set it level from the rims. The wheel should be a little finger's breadth above the bottom of the mortar. The wheels must be kept from grinding the mortar at all. Between the wheel and the central pillar there should be a finger's space. If there is more, and the wheels are too far off, wind a rope tightly round the pillar, close-coiled, to fill out the excess space. If the wheels are too high and grind the mortar too far down, set wooden discs, pierced, on the pillar at the central pillar, and so adjust the height. In the same way adjust the breadth with wooden discs or iron rings, until it is rightly fitted.

title: De Agri Cultura
text:
A crushing-mill was bought at Suessa for four hundred sesterces, and fifty pounds of oil; the fitting, sixty sesterces; the haulage by oxen, six days' work, six men with the ox-drivers, seventy-two sesterces; the bar, fitted, seventy-two sesterces; for the oil, twenty-five sesterces: total, six hundred and twenty-nine sesterces. At Pompeii one was bought, fitted, for three hundred and eighty-four sesterces; the haulage, two hundred and eighty sesterces; it is better put together and fitted at home, so there is a cost of sixty sesterces: total, seven hundred and twenty-four sesterces. If you procure wheels for old crushing-mills, make them a foot and three inches thick in the middle, a foot high, with a hole half a foot square each way. When you have brought them home, fit them to the mill. These are bought at the Rufrius quarries for one hundred and eighty sesterces, and fitted for thirty. They are bought at the same price at Pompeii.
23. See that what is needed for the vintage is got ready. Let the vessels be washed, the baskets mended and pitched, and the necessary jars pitched while it is raining; let the hampers be got ready and mended, the spelt ground, the small fish bought, the fallen olives salted. Gather the mixed grapes, the early wine for the labourers to drink, when the time comes. Divide the must, dry and clean, equally into the jars each day. If need be, add to the must boiled-down wine made from must that has been cooked off the lye: add a fortieth part of boiled-down must, or a pound and a half of salt to the culleus. If you add marble dust, add a pound to the culleus; put it into an urn, mix it with must, and pour it into the jar. If you add resin, take three pounds of resin to a culleus of must; pound it well, put it in a little basket, and let it hang in the jar of must; shake it often, so that the resin dissolves. When you have added boiled-down must, or marble, or resin, stir often for twenty days and pound it daily. Divide the last pressing of must, the run-off, separately into each jar and add it in equal measure.
24. Greek wine should be made thus. Gather well-ripened Apician grapes. When you have gathered them, into a culleus of their must put two quadrantals of old sea water, or a modius of pure salt; hang the salt in a little basket and let it dissolve in the must. If you wish to make helvolum wine, put in half helvolum and half Apician wine, and add a thirtieth part of old boiled-down must. Whenever you treat wine with boiled-down must, add a thirtieth part of it.
25. When the wine has matured and is being gathered, see that some is kept first for the household and your own people, and take care that you gather it well-ripened and dry, so that the wine may not lose its name. Sift the fresh grape-skins daily on a frame strung with ropes, or have a sieve made for the purpose. Tread them down into pitched jars or a pitched wine vat. Order this sealed up well, to give to the oxen through the winter. From the same, if you wish, you may wash off a little at a time: it will make second wine for the household to drink.
26. When the vintage is done, order the press vessels, the baskets, the hampers, the ropes, the props, and the fasteners each to be stored in its own place. See that the wine-jars are wiped out twice a day, and have separate brushes made for the purpose, with which to wipe round the rims of the jars. When the wine has stood thirty days, if the jars have been well cleared of skins, seal them up. If you wish to draw off the wine from the lees, this will be the best time for it.

title: De Agri Cultura
text:
27. Sow your seed: clover, vetch, fenugreek, beans, bitter vetch, fodder for the oxen. Make a second and a third sowing of fodder; then sow the other crops. Dig trenches in the fallow for olives, elms, vines, and figs; sow them together with the seed. If the place is dry, sow the olives at seed-time, and then prune low those that were planted before while they are still tender, and dig trenches round the trees.
28. When you plant olives, elms, figs, fruit trees, vines, pines, and cypresses, take them up carefully with their roots and with as much of their own soil as possible, and bind it round so that you can carry them; order them carried in a trough or a basket. Take care not to dig them up or carry them when there is wind or rain, for that is most of all to be avoided. When you set them in the trench, put the top soil at the bottom; then cover the roots with earth, then tread it down well with the feet, then ram it as hard as you can with rammers and bars: this will be the chief thing in the business. Trees more than five inches thick should be cut back before planting; smear the tops with dung and tie them up with leaves.
29. Divide the dung thus. Cart half of it onto the grain field where you sow fodder; and if there are olives there, dig trenches round them at the same time and add dung; afterwards sow the fodder. Add a quarter of it round the trenched olives, when there is most need, and cover the dung with earth. Reserve the other quarter for the meadow, and cart it out, when there is most need, while the west wind is blowing, at the new moon.
30. Give the oxen elm, poplar, oak, and fig leaves, as long as you have them. Give the sheep green leaves as long as you have them. Where you are going to sow, pasture the sheep there, and give them leaves until the fodder is mature. Keep the dry fodder that you store for winter as carefully as you can, and bear in mind how long the winter is.
31. Let what is needed for gathering the olives be got ready. Let the withies be ripe, the willow gathered in season, so that there may be material from which to make baskets and to mend the old ones. For fasteners, see that dry holm-oak, elm, walnut, and fig wood is thrown into dung or water; from these, when need arises, make the fasteners. Make levers of holm-oak, holly, laurel, and elm, and see that they are ready. Make the press-beam preferably of black hornbeam. Elm, pine, walnut, and all other such timber, when you dig it up, take out at the waning of the moon, after midday, when the south wind is not blowing. It will be ready when its seed is ripe; take care not to drag or hew it when there is dew. Timber that bears no seed is ready when the bark peels. When the south wind blows, take care to handle no timber, nor wine either, unless from necessity.
32. Begin to prune your vines and trees in good season. Layer the vine-shoots into the furrows; and so far as you can, train the vine upwards. Prune the trees in this way, so that the branches you leave are spread apart and are cut off cleanly, and so that not too many are left close together. Let the vines be well knotted; throughout all the branches take care not to throw down the vine nor to bind it too tight. See that the trees are well wedded to the vines, and that vines enough are attached; and where need be, let them be let down from the tree so that they may be pressed into the ground, and two years later cut off the old wood.
33. Tend the vineyard in this way. Tie up a well-knotted vine straight, so that it is not crooked, and always train it upwards as far as you can. Leave the fruit-bearers and the watch-shoots properly. Make the vine as tall as you can, and tie it up properly, but do not bind it too tight. Tend it thus. At seed-time dig trenches round the heads of the vines. Dig round a pruned vineyard, begin to plough, and draw continuous furrows back and forth. Layer the tender vines as soon as possible, and harrow them in. Trim the old wood as little as possible; rather, if need be, let it down and cut it off two years later. The time to cut back a young vine will be when it is strong. If the vineyard is bare of vines, set in furrows and there plant a rooted cutting; clear the shade from the furrows and dig often. In an old vineyard sow clover if it is lean (but do not sow anything that bears grain), and round the heads add dung, chaff, grape-skins, or some of these, that it may thrive the better. When the vineyard begins to leaf, thin the leaves. Tie up the young vines often, so that the stems are not broken; and when one has reached the trellis, tie up its tender shoots lightly and direct them so that they grow rightly. When the grapes begin to turn colour, bind up the vines, thin the leaves, expose the grapes, and hoe round the heads.

title: De Agri Cultura
text:
Cut the willow-bed in season, peel it, and tie it tightly. Keep the bark; when there is need for it in the vineyard, throw some of it into water and tie with it. Keep the withies for making baskets.
34. I return to seed-time. Wherever the ground is coldest and wettest, sow there first; in the warmest places the sowing should be done last. Take care not to handle rotten ground. In reddish soil, dark loam, gravelly, sandy ground, and likewise ground that is not wet, lupine will do well. In chalk, marshy ground, red soil, and ground that is wet, sow chiefly bearded wheat. Where the ground is dry and free of weeds, open and clear of shade, sow wheat there.
35. Sow beans in strong ground not subject to disaster. Sow vetch and fenugreek in places as free as possible of weeds. Winter wheat and wheat should be sown in an open, high place where the sun lingers as long as possible. Sow lentils in gravelly, reddish ground that is free of weeds. Sow barley in ground that is new or that can be cropped year after year. Three-month wheat should be sown where you have not been able to do the sowing in season, and where the ground, being rich, can be cropped continuously. Sow turnip, and the rape from which turnip-tops come, and radish, in well-manured or rich ground.
36. What manures the field. Pigeon dung should be spread on the meadow, the garden, or the field. Goat, sheep, and cattle dung, and likewise all other dung, keep carefully. Spread or water the trees with oil-lees: round the larger heads add amphorae of it, round the smaller, urns mixed with half their measure of water, after first digging round them, but not deep.
37. What is harmful to the crop. To handle rotten ground. Chickpea, because it is pulled up and is salt, is for that reason harmful. Barley, fenugreek, and bitter vetch, all these and all things that are pulled up exhaust the field. Do not put kernels into the crop.
What crops manure the field: lupine, beans, vetch.
What you may make dung from: straw, lupine, chaff, bean-stalks, husks, holm-oak and oak leaves. From the crop pull up the danewort, the hemlock, and round the willow-beds the tall grass and the sedge; lay these down as bedding for the sheep and oxen, together with rotted leaves. Sift out part of the kernels and throw them into a tank; add water and mix well with a shovel; from this add the mud round the trenched olives, and add the burned kernels likewise. If the vine is lean, cut up its own prunings small and plough or dig them in on the spot.
In winter do these things by lamplight: hew dry the props and stakes that you set under cover the day before, make torches, carry out the dung. But do not touch timber except between moons, at the half-moon. Whatever you dig up or cut off from the ground will be taken out best on the seven days immediately after the full moon. Take care above all not to hew, cut, or touch any timber, if you can help it, unless it is dry, and not when it is frosty or dewy. See that you hoe and weed the grain twice, and strip off the wild oats. From the pruned vines and trees gather up the prunings and make faggots, and stack the vine-prunings and the fig wood for the furnace, and the small logs in a pile for the master.
38. Make a lime-kiln ten feet wide and twenty feet high, and bring the top in to three feet wide. If you burn with one stoke-hole, make a large pit inside, big enough to hold the ashes, so that they need not be drawn out. Build the kiln well; see that the firebox encloses the whole bottom of the kiln. If you burn with two stoke-holes, there will be no need of a pit; when the ashes have to be dug out, dig them out at one stoke-hole, while the fire is in the other. Take care never to let the fire die out, and see that it is not interrupted by night or at any time. Put into the kiln good stone, as white and as little mottled as you can. When you build the kiln, make the jaws drop steeply downward. When you have dug deep enough, then make room for the kiln, so that it is as deep as possible and as little exposed to wind. If you have too shallow a place to build it, raise the top with brick, or smear the top on the outside with rubble and mud. When you have lit the fire, if any flame comes out except through the top opening, smear it with mud. Take care that no wind reaches the stoke-hole, and there guard above all against the south wind. This will be the sign that the lime is burned: the topmost stones should be calcined; likewise the lowest stones will fall calcined, and the flame will come out with less smoke.

title: De Agri Cultura
text:
If you cannot sell wood and twigs, and have no stone from which to burn lime, then burn charcoal from the wood; and the twigs and prunings that are left over from your use, burn on the field. Where you have burned them, there sow poppy.
39. When the weather is bad and work cannot be done, carry the dung out to the dung pit. Clean out the ox-stall, the sheepfold, the yard, and the farmhouse well. Bind the jars with lead, or tie them with green-dry oak. If you mend or bind a jar well, put a salve in the cracks, and pitch it well, you can make any wine-jar of it. Make the salve for the jar thus: a pound of wax, a pound of resin, two ounces of sulphur. Put all this into a new pot, add powdered gypsum till it has the consistency of a plaster, and mend the jars with it. When you have mended them, to make the colour match, mix two parts of raw chalk with a third of lime; from this make little bricks, bake them in the kiln, grind them, and apply the powder.
When it rains, look about the farmhouse for what can be done. So that there be no idleness, do the tidying. Bear in mind that even if nothing is done, the expense will be no less.
40. In spring these things should be done: furrows and trenches made, the ground turned for seed-beds and vine-nurseries, the vines layered; in rich, moist places elms, figs, fruit trees, and olives should be planted. Figs, olives, apples, pears, and vines should be grafted at the new moon, after midday, when the south wind is not blowing. Graft olives, figs, pears, and apples thus. The branch you are to graft, cut off and slope a little, so that water runs off; when you cut it, take care not to tear the bark. Take a hard slip, sharpen it to a point, and split a Greek willow. Add clay or chalk, a little sand and cattle dung, and knead these well together, so that it becomes as sticky as possible. Take the split willow and tie it round the cut stock, so that the bark does not break. When you have done this, drive the sharpened slip between the bark and the wood two first-finger-breadths in. Then take the slip of the kind you wish to graft and sharpen the end of it to a slanting point, two first-finger-breadths long. Take out the dry slip you have driven in, and put in its place the slip you wish to graft. Set bark to bark, and drive it in as far as you sharpened it. Do the same with a second, a third, a fourth slip: put in as many kinds as you wish. Tie more Greek willow round, smear the stock with kneaded mud three fingers thick, and over it tie an ox-tongue (the plant), so that, if it rains, water may not soak into the bark. Tie that ox-tongue over the bark, so that it does not fall off; then wrap and tie straw round it, so that the frost may not harm it.
41. There is one grafting of the vine in spring, another when the vine is in flower, and the latter is best. The grafting of pears and apples is in spring, also for fifty days at the summer solstice, and at the vintage. The grafting of the olive and the fig is in spring. Graft the vine thus: cut off the vine you are to graft, and split it down the middle through the pith; into it drive the sharpened slips, and when you graft them, set pith to pith. There is a second grafting: if vine touches vine, sharpen the tender wood of each obliquely, and tie them together, pith to pith and bark to bark. There is a third grafting: bore through the vine you are to graft with an auger, and into it drive two vine-slips of the kind you wish, cut obliquely, up to the pith; see that you join pith to pith, and drive in the one on one side and the other on the other side, where you bored. Make these slips two feet long, sink them into the ground, bend them back to the head of the vine, fix the middles of the vine in the ground with ties, and cover them with earth. Smear all this with kneaded mud, tie and cover it in the same way as the olives.

title: De Agri Cultura
text:
42. Graft figs and olives by another method. From whatever kind of fig or olive you wish, cut out the bark with a knife, and from the fig of the kind you wish to have, cut another piece of bark with a bud; fit it onto the place from which you cut the bark on the other kind, and see that it matches. Make the bark three and a half fingers long and three fingers wide. Smear and cover it in the same way as the rest.
43. If the place is wet, the trenches should be trough-shaped, three feet wide at the top, four feet deep, one foot and a palm wide at the bottom. Floor them with stone; if there is no stone, floor them with green willow poles laid crosswise; if there are no poles, with bundles of brushwood tied together. Then make planting-holes three and a half feet deep and four feet wide, and arrange that water runs from the hole into the trench; so plant the olives. For vines make trenches and layer-holes not less than two and a half feet each way. If you wish the vineyard and the olives you have planted to grow quickly, you should dig the trenches once a month, and round the heads of the olives every month, until they are three years old. Tend the other trees in the same way.
44. Begin to prune the olive grove fifteen days before the spring equinox. From that day you will prune rightly for forty-five days. Prune in this manner. Where the place is rightly fertile, take out whatever is dry and whatever the wind has broken. Where the place is not fertile, cut and plough it more. Clear the knots well and make the stems smooth.
45. Cut the olive sets that you are to plant in trenches three feet long, and handle them carefully so that the bark does not suffer when you hew or saw them. Those you are to plant in the nursery make a foot long, and graft them thus. Let the place be worked with the double mattock, the soil well softened and well crumbled. When you put in the set, press it down with the foot. If it does not go down far enough, drive it in with a mallet or maul, and take care not to split the bark as you drive it. Do not first make a hole with a stake into which to sink the set. If you plant it so that the set stands upright, it will live better. Sets are at last mature when they are three years old, when the bark turns. If you plant them in trenches or furrows, set three sets together and spread them apart, so that they project not more than four fingers above ground; or plant cuttings with eyes.
46. Make the seed-bed in this way. Choose the best, most open, and most richly manured place you can, and one whose soil is as nearly as possible like that where you are to set the plants, and so that the plants need not be carried too far from the seed-bed. Turn that place with the double mattock, clear away the stones, fence it well round, and plant in rows. Sink the set a foot and a half each way and press it down with the foot; if you cannot press it down far enough, drive it in with a mallet or maul. See that the plants project a finger's breadth above ground, smear the top of the set with cattle dung, set a mark by the set, and hoe often, if you wish the plants to grow quickly. Plant the other slips in the same way.
47. Plant reed thus: set the eyes three feet apart. Make and plant a vine-nursery in the same way. When the vine is two years old, cut it back; when three years old, take it up. If stock is to graze where you wish to plant the vine, cut it back three times before you set it by the tree. When it has five old joints, then set it by the tree. Plant leek every year, and every year you will have something to take up.

title: De Agri Cultura
text:
48. Make a seed-bed for fruit trees in the same way as for olives. Plant each kind of set by itself. When you plant cypress seed, turn the soil with the double mattock. Plant in early spring. Make the beds five feet wide; add fine dung; hoe and break up the clods. Make the bed level, a little hollow. Then sow the seed thick, like flax, and over it sift earth through a sieve a finger's breadth deep. Level that earth with a board or with the feet, fix forks round about, stretch poles across, and lay on brushwood or fig-wood hurdles to keep off the cold and the sun. Make it so that a man can walk underneath. Weed often. As soon as the grass begins to grow, take it out; for if you pull up the hard grass, you will pull up the cypresses with it. Sow and cover pear and apple seed in the same way. Sow pine-nuts in the same way, but like garlic.
49. If you wish to transplant an old vine to another place, you may, provided it is no thicker than an arm. First prune it back, leaving no more than two buds. Dig it well from the roots, follow out all the roots, and take care not to wound them. Set it in the trench or furrow just as it stood, cover it, and tread it down well; set up the vine in the same way, tie and bend it as it was, and dig often round it.
50. Manure the meadows at the new moon in early spring. Those that are not watered, when the west wind begins to blow and you fence off the meadows, clean and dig out by the roots all the bad weeds. When you have pruned the vineyard, make a pile of the wood and twigs. Prune the figs between, and in the vineyard trim the figs high, so that the vine may not climb them. Make seed-beds and repair the old ones. Do these things before you begin to dig the vineyard. When the sacrificial meal has been offered and eaten, begin the spring ploughing. Plough first the places that are driest, and plough last those that are richest and wettest, but not so late that they harden first.
51. The layering of fruit trees and other trees. The shoots that spring from the tree at the ground, press into the earth and raise the tip, so that it may take root; then two years later dig it up and plant it. The fig, the olive, the pomegranate, the quince and all other fruit trees, the laurel, the myrtle, the Praenestine nut, the plane — all these should be layered from the parent stock.
52. and taken up and planted in the same way. Those you wish to layer more carefully should be layered in pots or in pierced baskets and carried down into the trench with them. To make trees take root, pierce a pot; pass through its bottom, or through a basket, the branch you wish to take root; fill the basket or pot with earth, tread it down well, and leave it on the tree. When it is two years old, cut the branch off below the basket. Cut the basket through from the bottom all the way; if it is a pot, break it. With that basket or pot, set it in the trench. Do the same with a vine; a year later cut it off and plant it with the basket. In this way you may layer any kind you wish.
53. Cut the hay when the time comes, and take care not to cut it too late. Cut it before the seed is ripe, and store the best hay apart, for the spring ploughing, before you give the clover for the oxen to eat.
54. Fodder for the oxen should be prepared and given thus. When you have finished sowing, mast should be got ready and gathered and thrown into water. From this give each ox half a modius a day; and if they are not at work, it will be better to pasture them, or give a modius of grape-skins that you have stored in a jar. Pasture them by day; at night give one ox twenty-five pounds of hay. If there is no hay, give holm-oak and ivy leaves. Store all wheat and barley straw, bean husks, vetch and lupine husks, and likewise the husks of other crops. When you store straw, store under cover what is weediest and sprinkle it with salt, and then give it in place of hay. When you begin to feed in spring, give a modius of mast or grape-skins, or a modius of soaked lupine and fifteen pounds of hay. When clover is in season, give it first. Pluck it with the hands and it will grow again; what you cut with the sickle will not grow again. Give clover till it dries off, and so manage it. After that give vetch, then panic grass; after the panic grass give elm leaves. If you have poplar leaves, mix them in, so that the elm may go further. When you have no elm, give oak and fig. Nothing is more profitable than to take good care of the oxen. Oxen should not be pastured except in winter, when they are not ploughing; for when they eat green fodder, they always expect it, and you must muzzle them so that they do not strain after the grass while ploughing.

title: De Agri Cultura
text:
55. Store wood for the master under cover; pile the olive logs and roots in a heap under the open sky, in cone-shaped stacks.
56. The food allowance of the household. Those who do the work: in winter four modii of wheat, in summer four and a half; for the overseer, the overseer's wife, the foreman, and the shepherd, three modii. For the chained slaves, in winter four pounds of bread; when they begin to dig the vineyard, five pounds, until the figs begin to ripen; then go back to four pounds.
57. Wine for the household. When the vintage is done, let them drink second wine for three months; in the fourth month a hemina a day, that is, two and a half congii a month; in the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth months a sextarius a day, that is, five congii a month; in the ninth, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth months three heminae a day, that is, an amphora a month; and besides this, at the Saturnalia and the Compitalia, three and a half congii for each man: total wine per man through the year, seven quadrantals. For the chained slaves, add in proportion to the work they do; it is not too much for them to drink ten quadrantals of wine each in the year.
58. The relish for the household. Store as many of the fallen olives as you can. Afterwards store the ripe olives that will yield the least oil, and use them sparingly so that they last as long as possible. When the olives are eaten, give fish-brine and vinegar. Give each one a sextarius of oil a month. A modius of salt a year is enough for each.
59. Clothing for the household. A tunic of three and a half feet, and a cloak every other year. Whenever you give anyone a tunic or cloak, first take back the old one, to make patchwork of. Good wooden shoes should be given every other year.
60. The yearly fodder for the oxen, per yoke: one hundred and twenty modii of lupine, or two hundred and forty modii of mast; hay, four hundred and twenty pounds; clover; twenty modii of beans; thirty modii of vetch. Besides, see that you sow enough vetch for seed. When you sow fodder, make many sowings.
61. What is it to till a field well? To plough well. What is second? To plough. What is third? To manure. He who hoes his olive grove most often and deepest will plough out the finest roots; if he ploughs badly, the roots will run upward and grow thicker, and the strength of the olive will go into the roots. When you plough a grain field, plough well and in good season, and do not plough with a crooked furrow. For the rest of the cultivation, hoe much, take up the seedlings carefully, and in season carry as many roots as possible with their soil; when you have covered the roots well, tread them down well, so that water may not harm them. If anyone asks what is the time for planting the olive: in dry ground at seed-time, in rich ground in spring.
62. As many yoke of oxen, mules, or asses as you have, you should have just so many carts.
63. The press-rope should be stretched fifty-five feet; the leather cart-rope sixty feet; the binding-thongs twenty-six feet long; the cart yoke-straps eighteen feet; the cord fifteen feet; for the plough the yoke-straps sixteen feet, the cord eight feet.
64. When the olives are ripe, they should be gathered as soon as possible, and lie as short a time as possible on the ground and on the floor; on the ground and on the floor they rot. The gatherers want the fallen olives to be as many as possible, so that there is more to gather; the pressmen want them to lie long on the floor, so that they soften and are easier to work. Do not believe that oil can increase on the floor. The more quickly you press, the more it will profit you; from the same number of modii you will get both more oil and better. Olives that have lain long on the ground or on the floor yield less oil, and worse. Draw off the oil, if you can, twice a day; for the longer the oil stays in the lees and dregs, the worse it will be.

title: De Agri Cultura
text:
65. Make green oil thus. Take the olives off the ground as soon as possible. If they are dirty, wash them, and clean them of leaves and dirt. Press them the next day, or the day after they are gathered. When the olive is black, strip it. The more bitter the olive from which you make the oil, the better the oil will be. It is most to the master's profit that the oil be made from ripe olives. If there are frosts when you gather the olives, make the oil three or four days afterwards. If you wish, sprinkle these olives with salt. Keep the pressing-room and the cellar as warm as you can.
66. The duties of the watchman and the oil-drawer. Let him guard the cellar and the pressing-room carefully. Let him take care that as few as possible go into the pressing-room and the cellar. Let everything be done as cleanly and purely as possible. Let him not use a copper vessel, nor the kernels, for the oil; for if he does, the oil will have a bad taste. Set a leaden cauldron in the vat, into which the oil may flow. When the pressmen press with the levers, let the oil-drawer at once take up the oil with the shell, as carefully as he can, and not stop. Let him take care not to take up the lees. Put the oil first into one vat, then into another jar. From these vats always draw off the dregs and lees. When you have taken the oil from the cauldron, drain off the lees.
67. Again, the duties of the watchman. Let those who are in the pressing-room keep the vessels clean, and take care that the olives are well worked and well dried. Let them not cut wood in the pressing-room. Let them draw off the oil frequently. Let him give the pressmen for each pressing a sextarius of oil, and as much as is needed for the lamp. Let him throw out the dregs daily. Let him change the lees continually, until at last it reaches the vat that is in the cellar. Let him wipe the press-baskets with a sponge. Let him change the place of the oil daily, until it reaches the storage jar. In the pressing-room and the cellar let him take careful care that no oil is stolen.
68. When the vintage and the oil-making are done, raise the press-beams; hang the press-ropes, the mainstays, and the draw-ropes on the meat-rack or on the press; put back in its own place each of the discs, fasteners, levers, blocks, press-baskets, hampers, baskets, ladders, props, and whatever else has been used.
69. Treat new oil jars thus. Fill them with lees for seven days, and see that you keep filling up the lees daily. Then take out the lees and let them dry. When they are dry, soak gum in water the day before, and dilute it the next day. Then warm the jar, but less than if you wished to pitch it; it is enough that it be lukewarm; make it warm with a gentle fire. When it is moderately warm, put in the gum, and then smear it on. If you smear it rightly, four pounds of gum will be enough for a fifty-measure jar.
70. A medicine for the oxen. If you fear sickness, give to the healthy ones three grains of salt, three laurel leaves, three leek-fibres, three spikes of wild leek, three cloves of garlic, three grains of frankincense, three plants of savin, three rue leaves, three stalks of white vine, three white beans, three live coals, and three sextarii of wine. All these should be gathered, ground, and given in an elevated position. Let the one who gives it be fasting. Give of this draught to each ox for three days. So divide it that, when you have given to each three times, you use it all up; and see that both the ox itself and the one who gives it stand in an elevated position. Give it in a wooden vessel.

title: De Agri Cultura
text:
71. If an ox begins to sicken, give it at once one raw hen's egg; see that it swallows it whole. The next day grind a head of wild leek with a hemina of wine, and make it drink it. Grind it in an elevated position and give it in a wooden vessel, and let both the ox and the one who gives stand in an elevated position. Let the one who gives, fasting, give it to the fasting ox.
72. So that the oxen do not wear away their feet, before you drive them anywhere on the road, anoint the soles of their hooves with liquid pitch.
73. When the grapes begin to turn colour, give the oxen the medicine every year, so that they keep well. When you see a snake's skin, take it and store it, so that you need not look for it when there is need. Grind this skin, with spelt, salt, and thyme, all together with wine, and give it to all the oxen to drink. Through the summer take care that the oxen always drink good clear water: it matters for their health.
74. Make kneaded bread thus. Wash the hands and the mortar well. Put flour into the mortar, add water little by little, and knead it thoroughly. When you have kneaded it well, shape it and bake it under a crock.
75. Make a sacrificial cake thus. Crush two pounds of cheese thoroughly in a mortar. When you have crushed it well, put in a pound of wheat flour, or, if you wish it to be lighter, half a pound of fine flour, and mix it well with the cheese. Add one egg and mix it in well. From this make a loaf, lay leaves under it, and bake it slowly under a crock on a warm hearth.
76. Make a flat-cake thus. Two pounds of wheat flour for the base; for the sheets, four pounds of flour and two pounds of best groats. Soak the groats in water. When they are well softened, put them into a clean mortar and dry them well; then knead them with the hands. When they are well kneaded, add four pounds of flour little by little, and of both make the sheets. Lay them out in a basket to dry; when they are dry, lay them out neatly. As you make each sheet, when you have kneaded it, dab it with a cloth dipped in oil, wipe it round and grease it. When the sheets are ready, heat the hearth where you will bake, and the crock, well. Then sprinkle and knead in two pounds of flour, and from it make a thin base. Put fourteen pounds of sheep's cheese, not sour and quite fresh, into water; soak it there, changing the water three times. Take it out and dry it well, little by little, with the hands; when it is well dried, put it into a mortar. When you have dried all the cheese well, knead it together in a clean mortar with the hands and break it up as much as you can. Then take a clean flour-sieve and pass the cheese through the sieve into the mortar. Then add four and a half pounds of good honey; mix this well with the cheese. Then on a clean board, a foot wide, lay a band, place greased laurel leaves under it, and shape the cake. First lay single sheets over the whole base, then spread the mixture from the mortar over the sheets; add the sheets one by one, and smear each likewise, until you have used up all the cheese with honey. On top lay single sheets, then draw the base together and trim it; heat the hearth from the first in good time and adjust it; then set on the cake, cover it with a hot crock, and heap embers on top and round about. See that you bake it well and slowly. Open it, to look at it, two or three times. When it is baked, take it out and anoint it with honey. This will be a half-modius cake.
77. Make a spiral cake thus. As much as you wish, in proportion, make all the same as for the flat-cake, except shape it differently. Smear the base well with sheets and honey. Then handle it as you would a cord, and so lay it on the base, packing the single coils well and tightly. For all the rest, make and bake it as you would the flat-cake.

title: De Agri Cultura
text:
78. Make a tart thus. Make it in the band, with sheets and cheese, in the same way as the flat-cake, but without honey.
79. Make dumplings thus. Mix cheese and groats in the same way. From it make as many as you wish. Put fat into a hot copper pan; cook them one or two at a time, turning them often with two sticks; when cooked, take them out, anoint them with honey, sprinkle them with poppy, and so serve them.
80. Make a pour-cake in the same way as the dumplings, except have a cup pierced through and hollow. So pour into the hot fat. Make it handsome, like a spiral, and turn it with two sticks and present it. Likewise anoint it and brown it, but not too hot. Serve it with honey or honey-wine.
81. Make a pot-cake just like a flat-cake. Put into it all the same things as into a flat-cake. Mix it in a trough, put it into an earthen pot, lower this into a copper pan full of hot water, and so cook it over the fire. When it is cooked, break the pot, and so serve it.
82. Make a ball-cake just like a spiral cake, except shape it thus. From the sheets, cheese, and honey, make balls a fist high. Lay them close together on the base, arrange them in the same way as the spiral cake, and bake them likewise.
83. Make a vow for the oxen, that they may keep well, thus. To Mars and Silvanus, in the wood, by day, make a vow for each head of oxen. Three pounds of spelt, four and a half pounds of lard, four and a half pounds of meat, three sextarii of wine: these you may put into one vessel, and likewise put the wine into one vessel. A slave or a free man may perform this rite. When the rite is done, consume it at once on the spot. No woman is to be present at this rite or to see how it is done. This vow you may make every year, if you wish.
84. Make a custard thus. Mix half a pound of flour and two and a half pounds of cheese together, as for the sacrificial cake, with a pound of honey and one egg. Grease an earthen dish with oil. When you have mixed everything well, put it into the dish and cover the dish with a crock. See that you bake the middle, where it is deepest, well through. When it is baked, take out the dish, anoint it with honey, sprinkle it with poppy, set it under the crock a little while, and then take it out. So serve it with a little plate and a spoon.
85. Cook a Punic porridge thus. Put a pound of groats into water and let it soak well. Pour it into a clean trough; add three pounds of fresh cheese, half a pound of honey, and one egg, and mix all well together. So pour it into a new pot.
86. Make wheat-pudding thus. Put half a pound of clean wheat into a clean mortar, wash it well, rub off the husk well, and rinse it well. Then put it into a pot with clean water and cook it. When it is cooked, add milk little by little, until a thick cream is formed.
87. Make starch thus. Clean fine wheat well, then put it into a trough and add water to it twice a day. On the tenth day pour off the water, wring it out well, mix it well in a clean trough, and let it become like dregs. Put it into a new linen cloth and squeeze out the cream into a new pan or a mortar. Do all of it thus, and rub it through again. Set the pan in the sun to dry. When it is dry, put it into a new pot and cook it with milk.
88. Make white salt thus. Fill a clean amphora with its neck broken off with clean water and set it in the sun. Hang there a little basket of common salt and shake it and keep filling it up. Do this several times a day, every day, until the salt stops dissolving for two days. This will be the sign: drop in a dried fish or an egg; if it floats, the brine is ready, in which to preserve meat or cheese or salt fish. Set this brine in a basin or in pans in the sun. Keep it in the sun until it congeals; from this comes the flower of salt. When it grows cloudy, and at night, put it under cover; every day, when the sun is out, set it in the sun.

title: De Agri Cultura
text:
89. Stuff hens and geese thus. Shut up the tender hens that are first laying. Make pellets of barley meal or flour moistened with water, dip them in water, and put them in the mouth, adding a little more each day; judge by the throat what is enough. Cram twice a day, and at midday give them to drink, but let the water not stand by them more than one hour. Feed the goose in the same way, except give it to drink first, and twice a day, twice food.
90. Stuff a freshly caught ringdove thus. When it is caught, first give it cooked, toasted beans, blown from your mouth into its mouth, and likewise water. Do this for seven days. Then take clean ground beans and clean spelt, and let a third part of the beans come to the boil; then put in the spelt, do it cleanly, and cook it well. When you have taken it out, knead it well, grease your hand with oil, first a little, then knead it more, touch it with oil and knead it, until you can make pellets of it. Give it from water, and so adjust the feed.
91. Make a threshing-floor thus. Dig over the place where you will make it. Then sprinkle it well with oil-lees and let them soak in. Then break up the clods well. Then level it and beat it with rammers. Then sprinkle it again with oil-lees and let it dry. If you do this, neither ants will harm it nor weeds grow on it.
92. So that the weevil may not harm the grain, nor mice touch it. Make a mud of oil-lees, add a little chaff, let it soften well, and knead it well; with this thick mud smear the whole granary. Then sprinkle with oil-lees all that you have smeared. When it has dried, store the grain there cooled; the weevil will not harm it.
93. If an olive bears no fruit, dig a trench round it. Then lay straw round about. Then mix oil-lees with water in equal parts, and pour it round the olive. For a very large tree an urn of the mixture is enough; for smaller trees add in proportion. And if you do this same thing to fruitful trees, they too will be the better. Do not add straw to those.
94. That figs may hold their young fruit, do everything as for the olives, and besides, when spring comes on, bank earth well round them. If you do this, the unripe figs will not fall, the figs will not be scabby, and they will be far more fruitful.
95. That there be no caterpillar in the vineyard. Store oil-lees, make them quite pure, and put two congii into a copper vessel. Then cook over a gentle fire, stirring often with a little stick, until it is as thick as honey. Then take a third of a sextarius of bitumen and a fourth of a sextarius of sulphur. Grind each separately in a mortar. Then crumble them as finely as you can into the hot oil-lees, stir at the same time with the little stick, and cook again under the open sky; for if you cook it under cover, when the bitumen and sulphur are added, it will flare up. When it is as thick as birdlime, let it cool. Anoint the vine round the head and under the arms with this; no caterpillar will arise.
96. That the sheep may not become scabby. Store oil-lees, make them quite pure; mix together in equal parts the water in which lupine has been boiled and the dregs of good wine. Then, when you have sheared them, anoint them all over and let them sweat for two or three days. Then wash them in the sea; if you have no sea water, make salt water and wash them with it. If you do this, they will not become scabby, will have more and better wool, and the ticks will not trouble them. Use the same on all four-footed beasts if they are scabby.

title: De Agri Cultura
text:
97. With boiled-down oil-lees anoint the axle, the thongs, the shoes, and the leather: you will make all of them better.
98. That moths may not touch the clothing. Boil oil-lees down to half, and with it anoint the bottom of the chest, both inside and out, the feet, and the corners. When it has dried, store the clothing. If you do this, the moths will not harm it. And likewise if you anoint all wooden furniture with it, it will not rot; and when you have wiped it, it will become brighter. Likewise anoint all bronze, but first wipe it well; then, after you have anointed it, when you wish to use it, wipe it again. It will be brighter, and the verdigris will not trouble it.
99. If you wish dried figs to keep whole, store them in an earthen vessel. Anoint it with boiled-down oil-lees.
100. If you are going to put oil into a new jar, first rinse it with oil-lees just as they are, raw, and stir long, so that the jar soaks it in well. If you do this, the jar will not drink the oil, the oil will keep better, and the jar itself will be stronger.
101. If you wish to keep myrtle sprigs with their berries, and likewise any other kind you wish, and if you wish to keep fig twigs with their leaves, tie them together, make little bundles, and lower them into oil-lees; see that the oil-lees stand above them. But take those you mean to lower a little before they are ripe. Smear over well the vessel in which you store them.
102. If a serpent bites an ox or any other four-footed beast, take an acetabulum of the black cumin that the doctors call smyrnaean, grind it in a hemina of old wine, and pour it through the nostrils; and to the bite itself apply hog's dung. And do this same thing to a man, if need arise.
103. That the oxen may keep well and be in good condition, and that those which loathe their food may take it more eagerly, sprinkle the fodder you give them with oil-lees: at first a little, until they grow used to it, then more, and give it now and then to drink, mixed evenly with water. Do this every fourth or fifth day. So the oxen will be in better condition in body, and sickness will keep away.
104. Wine for the household to use through the winter. Put ten quadrantals of must into a jar; pour in two quadrantals of sharp vinegar, two of boiled-down must, and fifty of fresh water. Mix this with a stick three times a day for five days running. Add sixty-four sextarii of old sea water, put the cover on the jar, and seal it after ten days. This wine will last you until the summer solstice. Whatever is left over after the solstice will be the sharpest and finest vinegar.
105. On a farm far from the sea, make Greek wine thus. Pour twenty quadrantals of must into a copper or leaden vessel and put fire under it. When the wine boils, draw off the fire. When this wine has cooled, pour it into a forty-measure jar. Separately, in another vessel, pour one quadrantal of fresh water and one of salt; let it become brine. When the brine is made, pour it into the same jar. Pound in a mortar enough rush and sweet-flag, one sextarius, and pour it into the same jar, so that it may be fragrant. After thirty days seal the jar. In spring rack it off into amphorae. Let it stand set in the sun for two years. Then bring it under cover. This wine will be no worse than Coan.
106. The making of sea water. Take one quadrantal of sea water from the deep, where fresh water does not come. Roast a pound and a half of salt, put it in, and stir with a stick until a cooked hen's egg floats; then stop stirring. Pour into it two congii of old wine, either Aminnian or mixed white, and mix well. Then pour it into a pitched vessel and seal it. If you wish to make more sea water, do all this in proportion.

title: De Agri Cultura
text:
107. With what to smear the rims of the jars, so that they may be fragrant and that no fault may pass into the wine.
