Pour six congii of the best boiled-down must into a copper or leaden vessel, and pound as finely as you can, together with the must, a hemina of dried, crushed iris and five pounds of well-scented Campanian melilot; sift it through a sieve and cook it together with the boiled-down must over a brushwood and gentle flame. Stir it; see that you do not scorch it. Cook until you boil away half. When it has cooled, pour it into a pitched, well-scented vessel, seal it, and use it on the rims of the jars.
108. If you wish to test whether wine will keep or not, put half an acetabulum of coarse barley meal into a new little cup, and pour into it a sextarius of the wine you wish to test; set it on coals and make it boil twice or three times. Then strain it and throw away the barley meal; set the wine in the open air. The next morning taste it. If it has the taste of what is in the jar, know that it will keep; if it is sourish, it will not keep.
109. If you wish to make rough wine mild and pleasant, do thus. Make four pounds of meal from bitter vetch, and moisten it with four cyathi of wine and boiled-down must. Then make little bricks. Let them soak in night and day. Then mix them in the jar with that wine, and seal it after sixty days. This wine will be mild and pleasant, of good colour and well scented.
110. To take a bad smell from wine. Heat a thick, clean potsherd from a roof-tile well in the fire. When it is hot, pitch it, tie a little cord to it, and lower the sherd gently to the bottom of the jar; leave the jar sealed for two days. If the bad smell is taken away, that is best; if not, do it more often, until you have taken away the bad smell.
111. If you wish to know whether water has been added to wine or not, make a little vessel of ivy wood. Lower into it the wine you think has water in it. If it has water, the wine will run out and the water will stay; for an ivy-wood vessel does not hold wine.
112. If you wish to make Coan wine, take sea water from the deep when the sea is calm, when there is no wind, seventy days before the vintage, where no fresh water reaches. When you have drawn it from the sea, pour it into a jar; do not fill it, but let it be five quadrantals short of full. Put on a cover, leaving a vent to breathe. When thirty days have passed, pour it cleanly and gently into another jar, leaving at the bottom what has settled. After twenty days pour it likewise into another jar, and so leave it until the vintage. From the vines whose grapes you wish to make into Coan wine, leave the grapes on the vine, let them ripen well, and when it has rained and dried, then gather them and set them in the sun for two or three days under the open sky, if there is no rain. If there is rain, lay them out under cover on hurdles, and clean away any spoiled berries. Then take the sea water mentioned above; pour ten quadrantals of sea water into a fifty-measure jar. Then pluck the berries from the mixed grapes off the stem into the same jar, until you have filled it. Press the berries with the hand, so that they drink up the sea water. When you have filled the jar, cover it with a lid, leaving a vent to breathe. When three days have passed, take it out of the jar, tread it in the press, and store the wine in jars that are washed, clean, and dry.
113. That it may be well scented, do thus. Take a pitched potsherd, put a gentle ember on it, fumigate it with melilot, sweet-flag, and the palm that the perfumers have, set it in the jar and cover it, so that the scent does not escape, before you put in the wine. Do this the day before you wish to pour in the wine. Pour the wine from the vat into the jars as soon as possible, leave them covered for fifteen days before you seal them, leaving a vent to breathe; then seal them. After forty days rack it into amphorae, and add to each amphora one sextarius of boiled-down must. Do not fill the amphorae too full — up to the bottom of the handles — and set the amphorae in the sun where there is no grass, and cover the amphorae so that water does not get in; and do not leave them in the sun more than four years. After four years arrange them in a wedge-shaped pile and pack them tight.

title: De Agri Cultura
text:
114. If you wish to prepare wine that makes the bowels good, after the vintage, when the vines are trenched, trench and mark as many vines as you think enough for the purpose. Cut round and clear their roots. Pound black hellebore roots in a mortar, and lay these roots round the vine, and put round the roots of the vine old dung, old ashes, and two parts of earth. Throw earth over the top. Gather this wine separately. If you wish to keep it to old age for moving the bowels, keep it, but do not mix it with the other wine. Take a cyathus of this wine, mix it with water, and drink it before dinner. It will move the bowels without danger.
115. Throw a handful of black hellebore into an amphora of new must. When it has fermented enough, throw the handful out of the wine. Keep this wine for moving the bowels.
To prepare wine for moving the bowels. When the vines are trenched, mark them with red ochre, so that you do not mix it with the other wine. Lay three little bundles of black hellebore round the roots and throw earth over the top. At the vintage keep separately what you gather from these vines, and put a cyathus into the rest of the drink. It will move the bowels, and the next day purge them thoroughly, without danger.
116. How lentils should be kept. Dissolve laserwort in vinegar, mix the lentils with the laserwort vinegar, and set them in the sun. Then rub the lentils with oil and let them dry. So they will keep whole and well.
117. How white olives should be preserved. Before they turn black, let them be crushed and thrown into water. Change the water often. Then, when they are well soaked, press them out, throw them into vinegar, and add oil, with half a pound of salt to a modius of olives. Store fennel and lentisk separately in vinegar. If you wish to mix them in, use them soon. Pack them into a small jar. When you wish to use them, take them out with dry hands.
118. The white olive that you wish to use after the vintage, preserve thus. Add as much must as vinegar. Preserve the rest in the same way as is written above.
119. Make a relish of white, black, and mottled olives thus. Take the kernels out of the white, black, and mottled olives. Preserve them thus. Chop the olives themselves, add oil, vinegar, coriander, cumin, fennel, rue, and mint. Store them in a small jar, with the oil above. So use them.
120. If you wish to keep must the whole year, put the must into an amphora, pitch the stopper, and lower it into a pool. Take it out after thirty days. It will be must the whole year.
121. Make must-cakes thus. Sprinkle one modius of wheat flour with must. Add anise, cumin, two pounds of fat, a pound of cheese, and scrapings from a laurel twig, and when you have shaped them, put laurel leaves under them when you bake them.
122. To prepare wine for when urine passes too hard. Pound roe-deer plant or juniper in a mortar, put in a pound, and boil it down in two congii of old wine in a copper or leaden vessel. When it has cooled, put it into a flagon. Take a cyathus of this in the morning, fasting: it will help.
123. Make wine for sciatica thus. Cut up small a piece of juniper wood half a foot thick. Boil it with a congius of old wine. When it has cooled, pour it into a flagon, and afterwards use it, a cyathus in the morning, fasting: it will help.
124. Dogs should be shut up by day, so that they may be keener and more watchful by night.
125. Make myrtle wine thus. Dry black myrtle berries in the shade. When they are now dried like raisins, keep them until the vintage. Pound half a modius of myrtle into an urn of must, and seal it. When the must has stopped fermenting, take out the myrtle. This is good for an upset stomach, for pain in the side, and for the bowels.

title: De Agri Cultura
text:
126. For gripes, and if the bowels are loose, and if tapeworms and round worms are troublesome. Take thirty sour pomegranates, crush them, put them into a jar with three congii of dark, dry wine. Seal the vessel. After thirty days open it and use it; drink a hemina fasting.
127. To cure indigestion and strangury. When the pomegranate is in flower, gather it; pour three minae into an amphora, add one quadrantal of old wine and a mina of clean, crushed fennel root. Seal the amphora, and after thirty days open it and use it. When you wish to digest your food and pass urine, drink of this as much as you wish, without danger. The same wine purges tapeworms and round worms thoroughly, if you prepare it thus. Have the patient dine after fasting. The next day grind one drachma of frankincense, one drachma of cooked honey, and a sextarius of wine flavoured with marjoram. Give it to him fasting, and to a child according to its age three obols and a hemina of wine. Let him mount upon a stone roller and leap ten times and walk about.
128. To plaster a dwelling. Take earth as chalky or as reddish as possible, pour oil-lees onto it, and put in chaff. Let it soften for four days. When it has softened well, cut it up with a shovel. When you have cut it, plaster with it. So neither will the spray harm it, nor will mice make holes, nor will grass grow, nor will the plaster crack.
129. Make the floor where grain is threshed thus. Let the earth be dug over fine, sprinkled well with oil-lees, and let it soak up as much as possible. Break up the earth, and level it with a roller or a rammer. When it is levelled, ants will not trouble it, and when it rains, there will be no mud.
130. Sprinkle olive logs and other wood well with raw oil-lees and set them in the sun, that they may soak it up well. So they will not be smoky, and will burn well.
131. When the pear is in flower, make the sacrificial meal for the oxen. Then begin the spring ploughing. Plough first the places that are gravelly and sandy. Then, as each is heaviest and wettest, plough it last.
132. The sacrificial meal should be made in this manner. To Jupiter of the Feast offer a cup of wine, as much as you wish. Let that day be a holiday for the oxen and the ox-drivers and those who make the meal. When you are to make the offering, you shall speak thus: "Jupiter of the Feast, since it is fitting that a cup of wine be offered to thee for the feast in my house and household, for that reason be thou honoured by this offering of this feast." Wash your hands between, then take the wine: "Jupiter of the Feast, be thou honoured by the offering of this feast, be thou honoured by the wine set before thee." Give to Vesta, if you wish. The feast for Jupiter is a roast and an urn of wine. Offer it to Jupiter in purity, with due reverence. After the meal is made, sow millet, panic, garlic, and lentils.
133. The layering of fruit trees and other trees. The shoots that are born from the trees at the ground, press into the earth and raise up, so that they may take root. Then, when the time comes, dig them up and plant them rightly. The fig, the olive, the pomegranate, the sparrow-apple, the quince and all other fruit trees, the Cyprian and the Delphic laurel, the plum, the conjugula myrtle and the white and the black myrtle, the hazelnut, the Praenestine nut, and the plane — all these kinds should be layered from the parent stocks and taken up in this way. Those you wish to plant more carefully should be planted in pots. To make the trees take root, take a pierced pot or a little basket, pass a small branch through it, fill the basket with earth, tread it down, and leave it on the tree. When it is two years old, cut the tender branch off below and plant it with the basket. In that way you may make any kind of tree you wish take root well. Likewise layer the vine in a little basket, cover it well with earth, cut it off a year later, and plant it with the basket.

title: De Agri Cultura
text:
134. Before you reap, the preliminary sacrifice of a sow should be made in this manner. To Ceres, before you store these crops — spelt, wheat, barley, beans, rape seed — sacrifice a preliminary sow, a female pig. With frankincense and wine make an invocation beforehand to Janus, Jupiter, and Juno, before you sacrifice the female pig. Offer the heaped cake to Janus thus: "Father Janus, in offering thee this heaped cake I make good prayers, that thou mayest be willing and gracious to me and to my children, my house and my household." Offer the sacred cake to Jupiter and honour him thus: "Jupiter, in offering thee this sacred cake I make good prayers, that thou mayest be willing and gracious to me and to my children, my house and my household, being honoured by this cake." Then give wine to Janus thus: "Father Janus, as in offering the heaped cake I have well prayed good prayers, for the same reason be thou honoured by the wine offered." Then to Jupiter thus: "Jupiter, be thou honoured by that cake, be thou honoured by the wine offered." Then sacrifice the preliminary sow. When the entrails have been cut out, offer the heaped cake to Janus and honour him as you offered before. Offer the sacred cake to Jupiter and honour him as you did before. Likewise give wine to Janus and give wine to Jupiter, just as before for the offering of the heaped cake and the libation of the sacred cake. Then give entrails and wine to Ceres.
135. At Rome, tunics, togas, cloaks, patchwork garments, and wooden shoes; at Cales and Minturnae, hoods, iron tools, sickles, spades, mattocks, axes, harness, purple-edged work, and small chains; at Venafrum, spades; at Suessa and among the Lucanians, carts; threshing-sledges at Alba and Rome; jars and vats; tiles from Venafrum. Roman ploughs will be good for strong soil, Campanian for dark soil; Roman yokes will be best; the detachable ploughshare will be best. Crushing-mills at Pompeii and at the Rufrius quarry-wall near Nola; keys and locks at Rome; buckets, oil-urns, water jugs, wine-urns, and other bronze vessels at Capua and Nola; Campanian baskets are useful. Draw-ropes and all esparto-work at Capua; Roman baskets at Suessa and Casinum, though the best are at Rome.
If anyone is to make a press-rope, Lucius Tunnius at Casinum, and Gaius Mennius, son of Lucius, at Venafrum. For it eight good native hides should be used, fresh, well dressed, with as little salt as possible. They should first be dressed and greased with grease, then dried. The rope should be begun seventy-two feet long. It should have strands, with two thongs to each strand, two fingers wide. When it is twisted, it will be forty-nine feet long. Three feet will be lost in the splicing; forty-six will remain. When it is stretched, five feet will be added; it will be fifty-one feet long. A press-rope, stretched, should be fifty-five feet long for the largest vessels, fifty-one for smaller ones. The leather cart-rope, full length, sixty feet; the half-rope, forty-five feet; the binding-thongs for the cart, thirty-six feet; for the plough, twenty-six feet; the leading-thongs, twenty-seven and a half feet; the cart yoke-straps, nineteen feet; the cord, fifteen feet; the plough yoke-straps, twelve feet; the cord, eight feet.
Crushing-mills, of the largest size four and a half feet wide, the wheels three and a half feet high; the wheels of medium size, when taken from the quarry, a foot and a palm thick, between the central pillar and the rim two feet and two fingers, the rims a finger thick. The second-grade mill four feet and a palm wide, between the central pillar and the rim one foot and one finger, the rims five fingers thick, the wheels three feet and five fingers high, one foot and three fingers thick. Make the hole in the wheels half a foot square each way. The third-grade mill four feet wide, between the central pillar and the rim one foot, the rim five fingers, the wheels three feet and three fingers high, one foot and two fingers thick. When the crushing-mill has been brought to where you will set it up, fit and adjust it there.

title: De Agri Cultura
text:
136. On what terms a tenancy should be let on shares. On a farm at Casinum and Venafrum, in a good place, let him divide an eighth basket; in a fairly good place, a seventh; in a third-rate place, a sixth. If he divides the grain by the modius, a fifth. At Venafrum, in the best land, let him divide a ninth basket. If they grind in common, the tenant shall take to the mill the portion that is the tenant's share. Of barley let him divide a fifth by the modius, of beans a fifth by the modius.
137. The tending of a vineyard on shares. Let him tend well the farm, the orchard, and the grain field. On shares the hay and fodder enough for the oxen that are there; everything else in common, undivided.
138. It is permitted to yoke oxen on feast days. These things may be done: let them haul wood, bean-stalks, and grain that is not to be given out. For mules, horses, and asses there are no holidays, unless they belong to the household.
139. To thin out a sacred grove in the Roman manner, do thus. Make a sin-offering with a pig, and frame the words thus: "Whether thou be god or goddess, to whom this grove is sacred, as it is right to make to thee an offering of a pig as a sin-offering for the thinning of this sacred grove, and for these reasons, whether I or one at my bidding do it, that it may be rightly done, for that reason, in sacrificing this pig as a sin-offering, I make good prayers, that thou mayest be willing and gracious to me, my house and household, and my children: for these reasons be thou honoured by the sacrifice of this pig as a sin-offering.
140. If you wish to dig, make a second sin-offering in the same way, and add these words: "for the sake of doing the work." While the work goes on, do it daily, piece by piece. If you have left off, or a public or family holiday has come between, make another sin-offering.
141. The field should be purified thus. Order the suovetaurilia to be led round, with these words: "That with the favour of the gods all may turn out well, I charge thee, Manius, to see that this suovetaurilia purify my farm, my land, and my ground, in whatever part thou judgest they should be led round or carried round." Make an invocation with wine beforehand to Janus and Jupiter, and speak thus: "Father Mars, I pray and beseech thee to be willing and gracious to me, my house and our household; for which reason I have ordered the suovetaurilia to be led round my field, my land, and my farm, that thou mayest keep off, ward away, and turn aside diseases seen and unseen, barrenness and waste, calamities and storms; and that thou mayest let the crops, the grain, the vineyards, and the shrubs grow great and turn out well; that thou mayest keep safe the shepherds and the flocks, and give good health and strength to me, my house and our household: for these reasons, for the purifying of my farm, my land, and my field, and for the making of this purification, as I have said, be thou honoured by the sacrifice of these suckling suovetaurilia: Father Mars, for the same reason be thou honoured by these suckling suovetaurilia." Likewise with a knife see that the heaped cake and the sacred cake are at hand, and from these make the offering. When you sacrifice the pig, the lamb, and the calf, you should say thus: "and for that reason be thou honoured by the sacrifice of the suovetaurilia." It is forbidden to name Mars, or the lamb and the calf. If the offering is not wholly favourable for all, frame the words thus: "Father Mars, if anything in those suckling suovetaurilia has not satisfied thee, I make atonement with these suovetaurilia." If there is doubt about one or two, frame the words thus: "Father Mars, since that pig has not satisfied thee, I make atonement with this pig.

title: De Agri Cultura
text:
142. The duties of the overseer are these. Whatever the master has directed — all that should be done on the farm, whatever should be bought and got ready, and how the food and clothing of the household should be given out — I admonish him to see to and to do, and to be obedient to the master's word. Furthermore, how he should treat the overseer's wife, and how she should be commanded, so that on the master's arrival what is needed may be got ready and carefully tended.
143. See that the overseer's wife does the duties that are hers. If the master has given her to you as a wife, be content with her. See that she fears you. Let her not be too extravagant. Let her have as little to do as possible with the neighbour women and other women, and let her not receive them into the house or her quarters. Let her go nowhere out to dine, and not be a gadabout. Let her perform no religious rite, nor have one performed on her behalf, without the orders of the master or mistress. Let her know that the master performs the rites for the whole household. Let her be clean; let her keep the farmhouse swept and tidy; let her keep the hearth clean and swept all round each day before she goes to bed. On the Kalends, Ides, and Nones, and when a feast day comes, let her put a garland on the hearth, and on those same days let her make supplication to the household god according to her means. Let her see that food is cooked for you and the household. Let her keep many hens and have eggs. Let her have dried pears, sorb apples, figs, raisins, sorb apples in boiled-down must, pears and grapes in jars, sparrow-apples, grapes preserved in grape-skins and buried in jars in the ground, and fresh Praenestine nuts buried in a jar in the ground. Let her keep Scantian apples in jars, and the other fruits that are usually preserved, and the wild fruits — all these she should carefully keep stored every year. Let her know how to make good flour and fine spelt.
144. The gathering of olives should be let out in this manner. Let all the olives be gathered rightly, at the discretion of the master, or of whomever he has made watchman, or to whom the olives have been sold. Let no one strip or beat the olives without the orders of the master or the watchman. If anyone acts against this, no one shall pay for what he has gathered that day, nor shall it be owed. All who gather the olives shall swear to the master or the watchman that they have not stolen olives, nor has anyone by their fraud, from the estate of Lucius Manlius during this harvest. Whoever of them does not so swear, no one shall pay him for all he has gathered, nor shall it be owed. Let security be given for the right gathering of the olives, at the discretion of Lucius Manlius. Let the ladders be returned just as they were given, except those broken by age. If they are not returned, a fair deduction shall be made. If through the contractor's doing any loss has been caused to the master, let him make it good; this shall be deducted at the discretion of an honest man. Let him furnish as many gatherers and strippers as are needed. If he does not furnish them, the hire shall be deducted at the contract rate: so much less shall be owed. Let him not carry wood and olives off the farm. Whoever gathers the olives, if he carries them off, two sesterces shall be deducted for each carrying-off, and it shall not be owed. Let him measure all the olives clean by the oil-measure. Let him furnish fifty steady men, and two thirds of them strippers. Let no one combine to drive up the price for which the gathering and pressing are let, except whom he has named at the time as a partner. If anyone acts against this, if the master or watchman wishes, let all the partners swear. If they do not so swear, no one shall pay for that gathering and pressing, nor shall it be owed to the one who has not sworn. Allowances: for two hundred sesterces, five sesterces of salted olives, nine pounds of pure oil, and for the whole harvest five quadrantals of vinegar are added. For the salted olives they have not received, while they gather the olives, five sesterces shall be given for each modius.

title: De Agri Cultura
text:
145. The pressing of the olives should be let on this term. Let it be done rightly, at the discretion of the master or the watchman who has charge of the business. If six sets of vessels are needed, let it be done. Let him furnish such men as please the watchman or whoever has bought the olives. Let him make the crushing-mills ready. If labourers have been hired or the pressing let out, let payment be made for it, or it shall be deducted. Let him not touch the oil to use or to steal, except what the watchman or the master gives. If he has taken any, forty sesterces shall be deducted for each taking, and it shall not be owed. All the pressmen who have made the oil shall swear, either to the master or to the watchman, that from the estate of Lucius Manlius neither they nor any other by their fraud have stolen oil or olives. Whoever of them does not so swear, his whole share shall be deducted, and it shall not be owed. Let him have no partner except whom the master or the watchman has ordered. If through the contractor's doing any loss has been caused to the master, it shall be deducted at the discretion of an honest man. If green oil is wanted, let it be made. There shall be added oil and salt enough for his own use, two victoriati for vessels.
146. Olives on the tree should be sold on this term. The hanging olives on the farm at Venafrum shall be sold. Whoever buys the olives shall pay, beyond the price for which he bought, a hundredth part of the whole sum, and for the crier's fee fifty sesterces ready money, and oil: of the romanic, five hundred pounds, of the green, two hundred pounds; of the fallen olives, fifty pounds; of the stripped, ten pounds, to be measured by the oil-measure; of the unguent, ten pounds. By the master's weights and measures he shall give two cotulae of the first oil. The dates for payment, counting from the Kalends of November: in the tenth month for the gathering and pressing of the olives that have been let; and if the buyer has sub-let it, he shall pay on the Ides. He shall promise that these payments will be rightly made and done, and that surety will be given to the master or to whomever he orders, and shall give surety at the master's discretion. Until it is paid, or surety so given, whatever has been brought onto the farm shall be held as pledge; let him carry none of it off the farm; if he carries anything off, it shall belong to the master. The press-vessels, ropes, ladders, crushing-mills, and whatever else has been given him, let him return safe and sound, except what is broken by age. If he does not return them, let him pay a fair price. If the buyer does not pay the gatherers and pressmen who have done the work there, the one to whom payment is due, if the master wishes, let the master pay. Let the buyer owe it to the master, and give surety for it, and for this matter, as written above, let his goods likewise be held as pledge.
147. Hanging grapes should be sold on this term. Let him leave the unwashed grape-skins and the lees. Room for the wine shall be given until the first of October. If he has not removed it before then, the master shall do what he wishes with the wine. The rest of the terms as for the hanging olives.
148. Wine in the jars should be sold in this manner. For each culleus forty-one urns shall be given. That which is neither sour nor mouldy shall be given. Within the next three days let him taste it, at the discretion of an honest man. If he does not do so, the wine shall count as tasted. For however many days there has been delay through the master, so that he could not taste the wine, just so many days shall be allowed to the buyer. Let him receive the wine before the first of January. If he does not receive it before then, the master shall measure out the wine; whatever he has measured out, let him pay for it accordingly. If the buyer requires it, the master shall swear that he has dealt truly. Room for the wine shall be given until the first of October. If he has not removed it before then, the master shall do what he wishes with the wine. The rest of the terms as for the hanging olives.

title: De Agri Cultura
text:
149. The terms on which winter pasture should be sold. Let him state the bounds within which you sell. Let the grazing begin from the Kalends of September. Let him quit the dry meadow when the pear begins to flower; the watered meadow, when the upper and lower neighbour allow, let him then quit, or set a fixed day for both. The rest of the pasture let him quit on the Kalends of March. For two trained oxen and one gelding, when the buyer grazes, the master reserves grazing for himself. For greens, asparagus, wood, water, the path, and the cart-track, the master reserves the use. If the buyer, or the herdsmen, or the buyer's stock cause the master any loss, let him make it good at the discretion of an honest man. If the master, or the household, or the stock cause the buyer any loss, it shall be made good at the discretion of an honest man. Until he has paid the money, or given surety, or assigned a debtor, the stock and the household that are there shall be held as pledge. If there is any dispute about these matters, let the trial be held at Rome.
150. The yield of the sheep should be sold on this term. For each sheep a pound and a half of cheese, half of it dried; on feast days half the milk that he has milked, and besides one urn of milk: on these terms, that a lamb which has lived a day and a night counts in the yield; and on the Kalends of June let the buyer quit the yield; if there is an intercalary month, on the Kalends of May. Let him promise no more than thirty lambs. Ewes that have not borne shall count two for one in the yield. Let him sell the wool and the lambs, and let the collector remit it ten months hence. Let him pasture one late-born pig to every ten sheep. Let the contractor furnish a shepherd for two months. Until he has satisfied the master or paid him, let it be held as pledge.
151. How cypress seed should be gathered, sown, and propagated, and how a cypress grove should be planted, Minius Percennius of Nola showed thus. Tarentine cypress seed should be gathered in spring; the wood, when the barley turns yellow. When you have gathered it, set it in the sun and clean the seed. Store it dry, so that it lies out dry. Sow it in spring, in a place where the soil is most tender, of the kind they call dark loam, where there is water near. First manure that place well with goat or sheep dung, then turn it with the double mattock, mix the earth well with the dung, clear it of weeds and grass, and break up the earth well. Make beds four feet wide; make them slightly hollow, so that they can hold water; between them make furrows, by which you can clear the weeds from the beds. When the beds are made, sow the seed thick, as flax is usually sown. Sift earth over it through a sieve, a half-finger deep. Level it well with a board or with the hands or feet. Whenever it does not rain, so that the earth is thirsty, water the beds gently. If you have no means of irrigating, carry water and apply it gently. As often as need be, see that you add water. If weeds spring up, see that you clear them. Clear them while the weeds are as tender as possible, and as often as need be. Through the summer it should be done as has been said; and when the seed is sown, it should be covered with straw; when it begins to sprout, the straw should be taken off.
152. Concerning brooms of twigs, Quintus and Lucius Manlius showed thus. Within the thirty days in which you gather the wine, several times make brooms of dry elm twigs tied to a little stick, and with them rub the inner sides of the jars well all over, so that the lees do not cling to the sides.

title: De Agri Cultura
text:
153. Make wine of the lees thus. Have for this purpose two Campanian oil-baskets. Fill them with lees, put them under the press, and press them out.
154. How to measure out wine for the buyers without trouble. Make for this purpose a culleus-sized tub. Let it have four handles at the top, so that it can be carried. Pierce it at the bottom, and fit a pipe there that can be stopped tight; and pierce it at the top, up to where it will hold a culleus. Keep it set on a stand among the jars, so that the wine can run from the jar into the culleus. Fill it, then stop it.
155. Through the winter the water should be drained off the land. On the hillside keep the drainage-ditches clean. In early autumn, when there is dust, then is the greatest danger from water. When it begins to rain, the household should go out with iron tools and hoes, open the channels, lead the water out onto the roads, and see that it flows. In the farmhouse, when it rains, go round and see if it leaks anywhere, and mark the spot with charcoal, so that when the rain has stopped the tile may be changed. In the standing crops, in the grain, or in the field, or in the ditches, wherever water stands or anything blocks the water, it should be let out, the way opened, and the obstacle removed.
156. On the cabbage and its power to digest. Cabbage surpasses all vegetables. Eat it either cooked or raw. If you eat it raw, dip it in vinegar. It digests wonderfully, makes the bowels good, and the urine is wholesome for everything. If you wish to drink much at a banquet and to dine with pleasure, before dinner eat as much raw cabbage as you wish, with vinegar; and likewise, when you have dined, eat about five leaves: it will make you as if you had eaten nothing, and you will drink as much as you wish.
If you wish to purge the upper bowels, take four pounds of the lightest cabbage. From it make three equal handfuls and tie them up. Then set a pot with water on the fire. When it begins to boil, lower one handful for a moment, and the boiling will stop. Then, when it begins to boil again, lower it for a moment, while you count to five, and take it out. Do the same with the second handful, and likewise the third. Then put them together, crush them, take them out again into a linen cloth, and squeeze out the juice, about a hemina, into a little earthen cup. Into it put a grain of salt the size of a bitter vetch, and as much roasted cumin as gives a scent. Then set the cup in the open air at night. Whoever is to drink it, let him bathe in warm water, drink honey-water, and go to bed without dining. Then in the morning let him drink the juice and walk about for four hours, and attend to any business he has. When the urge comes and nausea takes hold of him, let him lie down and purge himself. He will throw off so much bile and phlegm that he will himself wonder where so much came from. Afterwards, when his bowels move downward, let him drink a hemina or a little more. If they move too much, take two conchs of fine flour, rub it into water, drink a little, and it will check it. But for those who are troubled with gripes, the cabbage should be soaked in water. When it is soaked, throw it into hot water and cook it until it is thoroughly soft, then pour off the water. Then add salt, a little cumin, and barley meal, and oil. Then bring it to the boil, pour it into a dish, and let it cool. Into it crumble whatever food he wishes, and then let him eat. But if he can eat the cabbage by itself, let him eat it. And if he is free of fever, give him dark, harsh wine, watered, to drink, as little as possible; if he has a fever, give water. Do this every morning. Do not give much, lest he grow sick of it, so that he may afterwards eat it gladly. Give it in the same way to man, woman, and child. Now concerning those who pass urine with difficulty and have it dribbling. Take cabbage, throw it into boiling water, cook it a little, so that it is half-raw. Then pour off the water, but not all. Add to it good oil and salt and a little cumin, and bring it to the boil a moment. Then let him sup the cold broth and eat the cabbage itself, so that it may digest as soon as possible. Do this daily.

title: De Agri Cultura
text: 157. On the Pythagorean cabbage, what good and what wholesomeness is in it. First you should know what kinds of cabbage there are and of what nature. It tempers everything for health and is ever changing with the heat, being at once dry and moist, sweet and bitter and sharp. But the seven good qualities that are spoken of in the mixture, the cabbage has all of them by nature. Now, that you may know their nature: the first is that called smooth; it is large, broad-leaved, with a great stalk; it has a strong nature and great power. The second is the curly, called parsley-cabbage; this is of good nature and appearance, and is stronger for healing than the one written above. There is also a third, called mild, with small stalks, tender, and the sharpest of all of these, of thin juice and most powerful. And know first that of all cabbages none is of such a kind for medicine. Apply it crushed to all wounds and swellings. It will cleanse all these sores and heal them without pain. It ripens swellings, brings them to a head, and will cleanse foul wounds and cancers and make them sound, which no other medicine can do. But before you apply it, wash with much warm water; then apply it crushed twice a day; it will take away all the foulness. The black cancer stinks and gives off foul matter; the white is purulent, but is fistulous and suppurates beneath, under the flesh. On wounds of this kind grind the cabbage, and it will make them sound: it is best for a wound of this sort. And if anything is dislocated, foment it twice a day with warm water, apply crushed cabbage, and it will heal quickly: apply it twice a day, and it will take away the pains. And if anything is bruised, it will break out; apply crushed cabbage and it will make it sound. And if a sore or a cancer arises in the breasts, apply crushed cabbage, and it will make it sound. And if the sore cannot bear its sharpness, mix in barley meal and so apply it. It will heal all sores of this kind, which no other medicine can do, nor cleanse. And for a boy or a girl, if there is a sore of this kind, add barley meal. And if you wish to eat it chopped, washed, dried, and sprinkled with salt and vinegar, nothing is more wholesome. That you may eat it the more gladly, sprinkle it with honey-vinegar; washed, dried, and sprinkled with chopped rue and coriander and salt, you will eat it a little more gladly. It will do you good, will let no evil settle in the body, and will make the bowels good. If there was any evil within before, it will heal it all, will draw all from the head and the eyes, and make them sound. This should be eaten in the morning, fasting. And if there is black bile, if the spleen is swollen, if the heart aches, the liver, the lungs, or the midriff, in a word it will heal all those things that ache within. Into it scrape some silphium; it is good. For when all the veins are puffed up with food, they cannot draw breath through the whole body, and from that some sickness arises. When the bowels do not move because of too much food, if you use cabbage in proportion, as I advise you, none of those sicknesses will come upon you. But for the disease of the joints nothing cleanses so well as raw cabbage, if you eat it chopped, with rue and chopped dry coriander and scraped silphium, and the cabbage sprinkled with vinegar, honey-vinegar, and salt. If you use this, you will be able to make trial of all your joints. There is no cost, and even if there were cost, you would still try it for the sake of health. This should be eaten in the morning, fasting. If anyone is sleepless or wasting, you may make him sound by this same treatment. But give to the fasting man roast cabbage, anointed and warm, with a little salt. The more he eats, the more quickly he will be made sound of that disease. For those troubled with gripes, do thus. Soak the cabbage well, then throw it into a pot and boil it well. When it is well cooked, pour off the water. Add good oil and a little salt and cumin and barley meal. Then bring it well to the boil. When it has boiled, put it into a dish. Give it him to eat, without bread if he can; if not, give him plain bread to soak in it. And if he has no fever, give him dark wine to drink: he will quickly be made sound. And if it should ever happen that someone is weak, this remedy can make him sound: let him eat cabbage as written above, and moreover keep the urine of one who has been eating cabbage, warm it, and set the man down in it; you will quickly make him sound by this treatment: this has been tried. Likewise, if you wash little children in this urine, they will never be weak. And those whose eyes are not clear, anoint them with this urine, and they will see better. If the head or the neck aches, wash it with this urine warm, and the aches will cease. And if a woman foments her parts with this urine, they will never grow inflamed; and she should foment thus: when you have heated it in a pan, set a pierced stool over it. Let the woman sit upon it, cover her, and put garments about her.

title: De Agri Cultura
text:
158. The bowels should be purged in this manner, if you wish to purge yourself well. Take a pot, add to it six sextarii of water and add a ham-hock. If you have no hock, add a piece of ham of half a pound, as little fat as possible. When it begins to be cooked, add two cabbage stalks, two beet stalks with their roots, a sprout of fern, not much mercury-plant, two pounds of mussels, a chub and one scorpion-fish, six snails, and a handful of lentils. Boil all this down to three sextarii of broth. Add no oil. From this take a sextarius warm, add a cyathus of Coan wine, drink it, rest a while, then again in the same way, then a third time: you will purge yourself well. And if you wish besides to drink Coan wine mixed, you may drink it. Of all these so many things, any one of them that is written, whichever you wish, can purge the bowels. But for this reason there are so many, that you may purge well, and it is pleasant.
159. A remedy for chafing. When you set out on a journey, keep a sprig of Pontic wormwood under your ring.
160. If anything is dislocated, it will be made sound by this charm. Take a green reed four or five feet long, split it down the middle, and let two men hold it at the hips. Begin to chant: "motas uaeta daries dardares astataries dissunapiter," until the ends come together. Brandish iron over it. When they have come together and one has touched the other, take it in the hand and cut it right and left; tie it to the dislocation or the fracture, and it will be made sound. And nonetheless chant daily, and over a dislocation in this way also: "huat haut haut istasis tarsis ardannabou dannaustra.
161. How asparagus is sown. The ground should be well worked, ground that holds moisture, or rich ground. When it is worked, make beds, so that you can hoe and weed right and left without treading on them. When you lay out the beds, leave an interval of half a foot between them on all sides. Then sow it; along a line, with a stake, drop two or three seeds, and with the same stake fill the hole with earth. Then sprinkle dung well over the beds. Sow just after the spring equinox. When it has come up, clear the weeds often, and take care not to pull up the asparagus along with the weeds. The year you sow it, cover the sown bed with straw through the winter, so that it is not nipped by frost. Then in early spring uncover it, hoe and weed it. After the third year from sowing, burn it over in early spring. After that do not hoe before the asparagus has come up, lest in hoeing you injure the roots. In the third or fourth year pull the asparagus from the root; for if you break it off, the stalks will form and die away inside. You may keep pulling it until you see it going to seed. The seed ripens in autumn. So, when you have taken the seed, burn it over, and when the asparagus begins to come up, hoe and manure it. After eight or nine years, when it is now old, divide it, and in the place where you mean to set it, work the ground well and manure it. Then make little trenches into which to sink the asparagus roots. Let there be an interval of not less than a foot between the asparagus roots. Pull it up; dig round it so that you can pull it up easily; take care that it is not broken. See that you bring in as much sheep dung as you can; that is best for the purpose; other dung breeds weeds.
162. The salting of hams and of the Puteolan brisket. Hams should be salted thus, in a jar or a storage-cask. When you have bought the hams, cut off their hocks. For each take half a modius of ground Roman salt. At the bottom of the jar or cask spread salt, then set down a ham, with the skin facing downward; cover it all with salt. Then set another on top, and cover it the same way; take care that flesh does not touch flesh. So cover them all. When you have now arranged them all, cover them over with salt, so that no flesh shows; make it even. When they have been five days in the salt, take them all out with their salt. Make the topmost ones lowest, cover and arrange them in the same way. After twelve days in all, take out the hams, wipe off all the salt, and hang them in the wind for two days. On the third day wipe them well with a sponge, anoint them with oil, and hang them in the smoke for two days. On the third day take them down, anoint them with oil and vinegar mixed, and hang them on the meat-rack. Neither moth nor worm will touch them.
